style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive text) + amplified study form; bare-transliteration in amp with Strong's carried in notes (matching the ch.1 pilot); em-dashes used sparingly.
chapterNote: The words of Agur son of Jakeh form an oracle of disciplined humility. He opens by confessing his own ignorance before the unsearchable Creator -- Who alone has gone up to heaven, gathered the wind, and bound the seas (vv. 1-4) -- and grounds all knowing in God's flawless, refining word (vv. 5-6). His one prayer is for the middle road of contentment, neither riches that breed self-sufficiency nor poverty that breeds theft (vv. 7-9). From there the chapter becomes a gallery of numbered sayings -- the famous 'three things, yea four' pattern -- cataloguing the insatiable, the arrogant, the wonderful, and the small-but-wise, until it ends with a plain warning: the man who churns up wrath will draw out strife as surely as a twisted nose draws blood (vv. 10-33).

1.text: The words of Agur the son of Jakeh -- the oracle. This man declares to Ithiel, to Ithiel and to Ucal:
1.amp: The words [dabar -- sayings, the burden of speech] of Agur the son of Jakeh -- the oracle [massa -- a burden, a weighty utterance laid upon the speaker]. The man declares [neum -- a solemn, prophet-like pronouncement] to Ithiel [Ithiel -- 'God is with me'], to Ithiel and to Ucal [Ukal];
1.notes: massa (H4853) is both a 'burden' and a prophetic 'oracle' -- the weighty word a prophet is given to carry; neum (H5002) is the formula of solemn declaration ('thus saith'). Agur (H94) and his hearers Ithiel (H384) and Ucal (H401) are otherwise unknown; the name Ithiel itself confesses 'God is with me,' fitting the humble awe that follows.

2.text: Surely I am too brutish to be called a man, and I have not the understanding of a human being.
2.amp: Surely I am more brutish [baar -- dull, stupid like a beast, void of reason] than any man [ish], and I have not the understanding [binah -- discernment] of a man [adam -- a human being, a son of Adam].
2.notes: baar (H1198) means brutish or beast-like -- stripped of human reason; binah (H998) is the discernment that distinguishes one thing from another. Agur opens not with boasting but with Socratic self-abasement before God, the true beginning of wisdom (cf. 1:7; Job 42:3).

3.text: I have not learned wisdom, nor do I possess the knowledge of the Holy One.
3.amp: I have not learned [lamad -- been trained in, schooled in] wisdom [chokmah -- skill in living], nor do I have the knowledge [daat] of the Holy One [qadosh -- the set-apart, sacred One].
3.notes: qadosh (H6918), 'the Holy One,' here stands for God Himself in His set-apart majesty; daat (H1847) is intimate, experiential knowing. Agur disclaims the self-made wisdom of the schools -- not to deny knowledge but to locate it wholly in God, who alone gives it (cf. 2:6; 9:10).

4.text: Who has gone up to heaven and come down again? Who has gathered the wind in the hollow of His hands? Who has bound the waters in a cloak? Who has set fast all the ends of the earth? What is His name, and what is His Son's name, if you know?
4.amp: Who has ascended [alah -- gone up] into heaven [shamayim] and descended [yarad -- come down]? Who has gathered [asaph -- collected, scooped together] the wind [ruach -- wind, breath] in His fists? Who has bound [tsarar -- wrapped, tied up] the waters in a garment [simlah -- a cloak, outer wrap]? Who has established [qum -- raised up, set firm] all the ends [ephes -- the farthest limits] of the earth [eretz]? What is His name [shem], and what is His Son's [ben] name, if you can tell?
4.notes: A cascade of unanswerable questions, like God's voice from the whirlwind (Job 38), exposing the creature's smallness before the Creator who alone holds wind (ruach, H7307) and sea. The startling final question -- 'what is His Son's name?' -- pushes beyond mere monotheism; Christian readers have long heard in it a foregleam of the eternal Son (cf. Ps 2:7; John 3:13, where Christ alone is the One who came down from heaven and ascended).

5.text: Every word of God is refined pure; He is a shield to all who take refuge in Him.
5.amp: Every word [imrah -- spoken word, promise] of God [Eloah -- God, the singular Almighty] is refined pure [tsaraph -- smelted and tested in fire, with all dross burned away]; He is a shield [magen -- a buckler, protector] to those who take refuge [chasah -- seek shelter, flee for cover] in Him.
5.notes: tsaraph (H6884) is the smith's verb -- to melt metal and skim off the impurities; God's imrah (H565) has passed through that fire and proved flawless (cf. Ps 12:6; 18:30). Against Agur's confessed ignorance (vv.2-3) stands this certainty: the tested word of Eloah (H433), and God Himself as magen (H4043) to all who run to Him for cover.

6.text: Do not add to His words, lest He rebuke you and you be exposed as a liar.
6.amp: Do not add [yasaph -- increase, append, do again] to His words [dabar], lest He reprove [yakach -- correct, convict, set right] you, and you be found a liar [kazab -- proved false, a deceiver].
6.notes: yasaph (H3254), to add, is forbidden because God's tested word (v.5) is already complete -- to supplement it is to impeach it (cf. Deut 4:2; Rev 22:18). The one who tampers will be convicted (yakach, H3198) and unmasked as a kazab (H3576), a liar; humility before the word means receiving it whole, not improving on it.

7.text: Two things I ask of You; do not withhold them from me before I die:
7.amp: Two things I have asked [shaal -- requested, inquired after] of You; do not withhold [mana -- keep back, refuse] them from me before I die:
7.notes: shaal (H7592) is the verb of petition; mana (H4513) is to hold back. Agur frames the only recorded prayer in Proverbs -- two linked requests offered with the urgency of a man conscious of his own death, and so of what truly matters.

8.text: Keep falsehood and lying words far from me; give me neither poverty nor riches -- feed me only with the bread that is my portion --
8.amp: Remove far [rachaq -- put at a distance, banish] from me vanity [shav -- emptiness, worthless deception] and lying words [kazab]; give [natan] me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food [lechem -- bread, daily fare] that is my appointed measure [choq -- my prescribed allotment, my set portion];
8.notes: shav (H7723) is emptiness or falseness, often paired with idolatry; the first request is for a true tongue and a true heart. choq (H2706) means a 'statute' or fixed allotment -- 'the bread of my portion,' just what is decreed for the day (cf. Matt 6:11, 'give us this day our daily bread'). The second request is for the contented middle, neither extreme.

9.text: lest I be full and disown You and say, 'Who is the LORD?' or lest I be poor and steal, and so profane the name of my God.
9.amp: lest I be full [saba -- sated, satisfied] and deny [kachash -- disown, repudiate] You, and say, 'Who is the LORD [YHWH]?' or lest I be poor and steal [ganab -- thieve], and lay hold of [taphas -- seize, grasp, handle] the name [shem] of my God [Elohim] in vain.
9.notes: the prayer's wisdom is in its motive: saba (H7646), being full, breeds the proud question 'Who is YHWH?' (cf. Deut 8:12-14; Exod 5:2), while desperate poverty drives a man to ganab (H1589) and so to drag God's shem (H8034) into his crime. Both extremes endanger faith; the middle road guards it.

10.text: Never carry a servant's name to his master with malice; if you do, his curse will fall back on you, and the guilt of it will be yours to carry.
10.amp: Do not slander [accuse falsely with the tongue] a servant [ebed -- a slave, a bondman] to his master [adon -- lord, owner], lest he curse [qalal -- revile, call down evil on] you, and you be found guilty [asham -- bear guilt, be held in the wrong].
10.notes: the Hebrew idiom is 'do not hurt with your tongue' -- to inform against a lowly ebed (H5650) and harm one who cannot answer back. The wronged servant's qalal (H7043), his curse, will recoil, and the slanderer himself will bear the asham (H816), the guilt -- a warning against careless cruelty toward the defenseless.

11.text: There is a breed of men that curses its father and does not bless its mother;
11.amp: There is a generation [dor -- a kind, a class, an age of people] that curses [qalal -- reviles, treats with contempt] its father [ab], and does not bless [barak -- speak well of, honor] its mother [em].
11.notes: dor (H1755) here means not an era but a recurring 'breed' or type of person; four such breeds are catalogued in vv.11-14. The first sin against the fifth commandment heads the list -- to qalal (H7043) a father and refuse to barak (H1288) a mother is to overturn the very root of covenant order (cf. 20:20; Exod 20:12).

12.text: a breed that is clean in its own eyes, yet is not washed of its filth;
12.amp: There is a generation [dor] that is pure [tahor -- ceremonially clean, undefiled] in its own eyes [ayin], yet is not washed [rachats] from its filthiness [the foulness of its excrement, its moral dung].
12.notes: tahor (H2889) is the priestly word for 'clean' -- but self-declared, in its own ayin (H5869), not before God. The stark image is of one who fancies himself spotless while still caked in filth (cf. Luke 18:11; Rev 3:17). Self-righteousness is its own kind of uncleanness, the more dangerous for being unfelt.

13.text: a breed -- how lofty are its eyes, how raised its haughty stare!
13.amp: There is a generation [dor] -- oh how lofty [rum -- high, lifted up, exalted] are its eyes [ayin]! -- and its eyelids [aphaph -- eyelids, the proud gaze] are lifted up [nasa -- raised, held high].
13.notes: rum (H7311), to be high, and nasa (H5375), to lift, together paint arrogance as a posture of the eyes (ayin, H5869) -- the proud look God hates first among the seven abominations (6:17). The haughty stare that looks down on all others is the visible mark of this third breed.

14.text: a breed whose teeth are swords and whose jaws are knives, to devour the poor off the earth and the needy from among mankind.
14.amp: There is a generation [dor] whose teeth [shen] are as swords [chereb], and its jaw-teeth as knives [maakeleth -- a slaughtering blade, the knife for sacrifice], to devour [akal -- eat up, consume] the poor [ani -- the afflicted, the humble] off the earth [eretz], and the needy [evyon -- the destitute] from among men [adam].
14.notes: the climax of the four breeds: cruelty armed for cannibal feeding. maakeleth (H3979) is the very knife Abraham raised over Isaac (Gen 22:10) -- here turned on the helpless. To akal (H398) the ani (H6041) and evyon (H34) is to make oppression a meal; the breed that despises parents and exalts itself ends by eating the poor alive.

15.text: The leech has two daughters, crying, 'Give! Give!' There are three things never satisfied, four that never say, 'Enough!':
15.amp: The leech [bloodsucker] has two daughters [bath], crying, 'Give [yahab -- hand it over], give!' There are three [shalosh] things that are never satisfied [saba -- filled, sated], four [arba] that never say, 'Enough [hon -- wealth, plenty]':
15.notes: the leech's two 'daughters' are her twin suckers, forever demanding yahab (H3051), 'give!' -- a parable of greed that can never be filled (saba, H7646). The 'three... yea four' formula (cf. Amos 1) names a category and then drives past it; here the theme is insatiability -- appetites that, like Sheol, are bottomless.

16.text: the grave; the barren womb; the land never sated with water; and the fire that never says, 'Enough!'
16.amp: The grave [sheol -- the realm of the dead, the pit]; the barren [closed, childless] womb [racham]; the earth [eretz] that is not filled [saba] with water [mayim]; and the fire [esh] that never says, 'Enough [hon]!'
16.notes: four bottomless mouths: Sheol (H7585) that swallows every generation, the racham (H7356) -- the very word for tender 'compassion,' here a womb aching to bear -- the cracked, thirsty land, and devouring fire. Each receives endlessly and is never full; together they teach the heart to beware the appetite that knows no 'enough.'

17.text: The eye that mocks a father and scorns to obey a mother -- the ravens of the valley will peck it out, and the young eagles will devour it.
17.amp: The eye [ayin] that mocks [scoffs, holds in derision] at his father [ab], and despises [buz -- treats with contempt] to obey [yiqqahah -- the obedience, the dutiful heeding owed] his mother [em], the ravens [oreb] of the valley [nachal -- the wadi, the dry streambed] shall pick it out, and the young eagles [nesher -- eagle, vulture] shall eat it.
17.notes: the punishment fits the organ of the crime: the scornful ayin (H5869) that despised (buz, H936) its mother becomes carrion for valley ravens and vultures -- the corpse of the dishonoring son left unburied, the worst of fates (cf. 1 Kgs 14:11). Contempt for parents (echoing v.11) reaps a death stripped of all honor.

18.text: Three things are too wonderful for me, four I cannot comprehend:
18.amp: There are three [shalosh] things which are too wonderful [pala -- marvelous, beyond grasp, past human power to do] for me, yea four [arba] which I do not know [yada -- understand, fathom]:
18.notes: pala (H6381) names what surpasses human ability -- the same root used of God's 'wonders.' Agur returns from satire to awe: a numbered list not of evils but of mysteries, things that leave no trace and so escape his understanding (yada, H3045).

19.text: the way of an eagle in the sky; the way of a serpent on a rock; the way of a ship in the heart of the sea; and the way of a man with a maiden.
19.amp: The way [derek -- path, manner, track] of an eagle [nesher] in the heavens [shamayim]; the way [derek] of a serpent [nachash] upon a rock [tsur -- crag, cliff]; the way [derek] of a ship [oniyyah] in the heart [leb -- the midst] of the sea [yam]; and the way [derek] of a man [geber -- a strong man] with a maiden [an unmarried young woman].
19.notes: the unifying wonder is the trackless path -- derek (H1870) repeated four times for motion that leaves no mark behind: the eagle's wake in air, the snake's glide on bare stone, the ship's furrow that closes over the sea's leb (H3820). The fourth, the way of a geber (H1397) with a maiden, crowns them: the mystery of courtship and love, untraceable as the rest.

20.text: Such is how the adulteress goes about it: when she has finished, she dabs her mouth clean and protests, 'There is no wrong in anything I have done.'
20.amp: Such is the way [derek] of an adulterous [naaph -- one who commits adultery] woman [ishshah]: she eats [akal], and wipes [machah -- blots out, wipes clean] her mouth [peh], and says, 'I have done [paal -- worked, accomplished] no wickedness [aven -- iniquity, wrong].'
20.notes: set in dark contrast to v.19: the same word derek (H1870), but here a 'way' that is no innocent mystery. The adulteress treats her sin as casually as a meal -- eats, wipes her peh (H6310) clean, and denies any aven (H205). machah (H4229), to wipe away, hides the act and sears the conscience; the wonder of love (v.19) has a counterfeit that feels nothing.

21.text: There are three things that set the earth to shaking, and a fourth whose weight it has no strength to carry:
21.amp: For three [shalosh] things the earth [eretz] is disquieted [ragaz -- quakes, shakes, is set trembling], and for four [arba] which it cannot [yakol -- is unable, has not strength to] bear [nasa -- carry, endure]:
21.notes: ragaz (H7264) is to quake or shudder -- the very ground convulsing under what is intolerable. The list names not natural disasters but social inversions: things so out of order that creation itself cannot nasa (H5375), cannot bear the weight (cf. the 'three... four' overload of vv.15, 18, 29).

22.text: under a servant when he becomes king, and a fool when he is filled with food;
22.amp: For a servant [ebed -- a slave] when he reigns [malak -- becomes king, takes the throne]; and a fool [nabal -- a senseless, godless brute] when he is filled [saba] with food [lechem];
22.notes: the nabal (H5036) is not the simple-minded but the morally coarse fool (cf. 1 Sam 25); to fill such a man with plenty (saba, H7646) is to arm folly with power. An ebed (H5650) suddenly enthroned and a brute suddenly sated both lack the formation that station requires -- power without character that the earth groans to carry.

23.text: under an unloved woman when at last she is married, and a maidservant who dispossesses her mistress.
23.amp: For a hateful [sane -- odious, unloved, passed over] woman when she is married [baal -- taken as wife, mastered, owned]; and a handmaid [a servant-girl] who is heir [yarash -- dispossesses, takes the inheritance] to her mistress.
23.notes: sane (H8130) is to be hated or unloved -- the long-spurned woman whose sudden marriage breeds bitterness; baal (H1166) is to become a husband/master. The maidservant who displaces (yarash, H3423) her mistress (cf. Hagar and Sarah, Gen 16) completes the picture: each is a reversal that intoxicates the one lifted and embitters the world around -- order overturned past bearing.

24.text: Four things on the earth are small, yet they are wise, made wise beyond the wise:
24.amp: There are four [arba] things which are little [qatan -- small, slight, of no account] upon the earth [eretz], but they are exceeding wise [chakam -- skilled, made wise, prudent]:
24.notes: a turn from the unbearable to the admirable: the qatan (H6996), the small and overlooked, schooling the proud. These four creatures lack size and strength yet possess chokmah in action -- chakam (H2449), 'wise, made wise' -- proving that true wisdom is not grandeur but the skilled use of what one has (cf. the ant of 6:6).

25.text: the ants are a people without strength, yet they store up their food in the summer;
25.amp: The ants [nemalah] are a people [am -- a nation, a folk] not strong [robust, mighty], yet they prepare [kun -- establish, lay up, make ready] their food [lechem] in the summer [qayits -- summer, the harvest season];
25.notes: the first wisdom is foresight: the ant, an am (H5971) without power, reads the season and lays up provision (kun, H3559) before the need (cf. 6:6-8). Wisdom is not strength but timely diligence -- working with the season instead of against it.

26.text: the rock badgers, for all their weakness as a people, still set their dwellings deep within the cliffs;
26.amp: The conies [rock badgers, the shaphan] are but a feeble [not powerful] folk [am], yet they make [sum -- set, place, fix] their houses [bayith] in the rocks [sela -- crag, cliff, stronghold];
26.notes: the second wisdom is refuge: a feeble am (H5971) compensates for weakness by setting its bayith (H1004) in the unassailable sela (H5553), the cliff-rock that is elsewhere a name for God Himself (Ps 18:2). The wise know their limits and shelter in what is stronger than they are.

27.text: the locusts have no king, yet they all go out in ranks;
27.amp: The locusts [arbeh -- the swarming locust] have no king [melek], yet they all go forth [yatsa -- advance, march out] in bands [in ranks, divided and ordered like an army];
27.notes: the third wisdom is ordered unity: the arbeh (H697) swarm moves as a disciplined host though it has no melek (H4428) to command it (cf. Joel 2:7-8). Wisdom can produce concerted, ranked action by shared instinct and order, not only by a ruler's whip.

28.text: the lizard you can grasp in your hands, yet it is found in the palaces of kings.
28.amp: The lizard [the gecko] takes hold [taphas -- seizes, grips, clings] with its hands, and is in kings' [melek] palaces [hekal -- palace, great house, temple-hall].
28.notes: the fourth wisdom is bold access: a creature small enough to catch in the hand (taphas, H8610), yet by daring and grip it dwells in the hekal (H1964), the king's own hall. The least, by audacity, reaches the highest place -- a quiet rebuke to those who think only the great belong among the great.

29.text: Three things are stately in their stride, four are stately in their going:
29.amp: There are three [shalosh] things which are stately [yatab -- go well, move with grace] in their march, yea four [arba] which are comely [tob -- good, beautiful, fine] in their going [yalak -- walking, moving forward]:
29.notes: the final numbered set turns from the small-and-wise to the great-and-dignified -- creatures tob (H2895) in the very manner of their walking (yalak, H3212). The theme is bearing, the unhurried majesty of those who move as if they answer to no one.

30.text: the lion, mightiest among beasts, who turns back before nothing;
30.amp: A lion [layish -- a strong, full-grown lion], which is strongest [gibbor -- mighty, a warrior] among beasts [behemah -- animals, cattle], and turns not away [shub -- retreats not, does not turn back] before [panim -- the face of] any;
30.notes: the lion is gibbor (H1368), a 'mighty warrior' among beasts (behemah, H929), and refuses to shub (H7725) -- to turn back -- before the face (panim, H6440) of any creature. Fearless majesty heads the list; the same lion-imagery is later given to Judah's King and to the Lion of Judah (Gen 49:9; Rev 5:5).

31.text: the strutting rooster, the he-goat, and a king secure with his troops around him.
31.amp: The greyhound [one girt in the loins -- a strutting cock or war-horse, the bold-striding one]; the male goat [the he-goat that leads the flock] also; and a king [melek] against whom there is no rising up [alqum -- none can stand, irresistible, with his army about him].
31.notes: the Hebrew of the first term is uncertain -- 'girt in the loins,' rendered as the strutting rooster or a war-horse -- joined to the he-goat that walks at the flock's head. The climax is the melek (H4428) in his secure majesty; alqum (H510) suggests 'no resistance,' the king flanked by his host whom none dare oppose. From beast to leader, the gallery rises to the dignity of rightful rule.

32.text: If you have been foolish in exalting yourself, or if you have schemed evil -- clap your hand over your mouth.
32.amp: If you have done foolishly [nabel -- acted senselessly, played the fool, brought yourself to shame] in lifting up [nasa -- exalting, raising] yourself, or if you have thought [zamam -- plotted, devised] evil, lay your hand upon your mouth [peh].
32.notes: the chapter's penultimate word is restraint: nabel (H5034), to act the fool and wither one's own honor, whether by self-exaltation (nasa, H5375) or by scheming (zamam, H2161) evil. The cure is silence -- the hand clapped over the peh (H6310), stopping the boast or the plot before it escapes (cf. Job 40:4). Wisdom often shows first as a closed mouth.

33.text: For as pressing milk brings forth curds, and twisting the nose brings forth blood, so pressing out anger brings forth strife.
33.amp: Surely the churning [pressing, squeezing] of milk [chalab] brings forth [yatsa -- produces, draws out] butter [curds], and the wringing [the same pressing] of the nose [aph -- nostril, and so anger] brings forth [yatsa] blood [dam], so the forcing [the same pressing] of wrath [aph -- nose, nostril; kindled anger] brings forth [yatsa] strife [rib -- quarrel, contention, legal dispute].
33.notes: the closing proverb turns on one repeated verb of pressure and a brilliant pun: aph (H639) means both 'nose' and 'anger.' Squeeze (yatsa, H3318) milk and you get curds; squeeze the aph (the nose) and you get blood; squeeze the aph (the temper) and you get rib (H7379), strife. Pressure produces according to its kind -- so the man who keeps pressing his anger will inevitably draw out conflict, as surely as a wrung nose bleeds.
